summary: H.R. 10369, the Net Effective Cost Transparency and Prescription Drug Affordability Act of 2026, establishes new transparency, bidding, and oversight requirements for pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) working with Medicare prescription drug plans (Part D), Medicare Advantage plans, and commercial health plans governed by ERISA. The bill requires standardized bidding processes, regular reporting of actual versus projected costs, audits of plan sponsors, penalties for inaccurate bids or excessive cost variances, and incorporates performance measures into star rating systems for health plans.

affected_groups.effect: Must participate in standardized bidding processes, provide detailed cost and price concession breakdowns, guarantee net effective costs under threat of contract termination or penalties, and comply with new transparency standards.

Must solicit standardized bids, submit comprehensive documentation to the Secretary, maintain real-time cost-sharing tools and escrow accounts for refunds, and undergo regular audits and reconciliations.
affected_groups.group: Medicare Part D and Medicare Advantage Plan Sponsors

affected_groups.effect: Receive protections against unexpected cost-sharing increases, benefit from real-time cost-sharing tools, and get notifications if their plan receives low performance ratings on prescription drug cost measures.
Must receive projected net effective cost descriptions in a uniform format from service providers for bids submitted by PBMs.

key_provisions: Requires Medicare Part D plan sponsors, starting January 1, 2028, to use a standardized public bidding process for pharmacy benefit management services and accept all conforming bids.

Mandates that if a plan sponsor selects a PBM bid that does not have the lowest projected net effective cost, the selection must be justified as necessary to advance a significant programmatic interest and approved by the Secretary.

Establishes enhanced oversight, annual audits for at least one-third of PDP sponsors, quarterly variance analyses, and risk-based monitoring when actual costs diverge from projected costs by more than an established percentage.

Imposes civil monetary penalties (up to $100,000 for false or misleading information, and $25,000 per day for failing to provide required information) and allows the Secretary to require restitution and refunds for plan enrollees.

Creates a prescription drug cost performance measure and a 5-star rating scale for Medicare Advantage-PD and Part D plans, integrating the measure into overall star ratings and quality bonus payments.

Requires pharmacy benefit managers to guarantee that actual net effective costs will not exceed projected net effective costs by more than an established percentage, permitting plan sponsors to terminate contracts without penalty if breached.

Amends the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) to require covered service providers to include descriptions of projected net effective costs for bids received from PBMs, and defines bona fide service fees.
missing_information: The exact percentage threshold (not to exceed 10 percent) that the Secretary will establish for acceptable variance between projected and actual net effective costs.
The exact dates and rulemaking details for several administrative regulations to be promulgated by the Secretary within 180 days of enactment.
summary_detail.plain_summary: H.R. 10369, the Net Effective Cost Transparency and Prescription Drug Affordability Act of 2026, establishes new transparency, bidding, and oversight requirements for pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) working with Medicare prescription drug plans (Part D), Medicare Advantage plans, and commercial health plans governed by ERISA. The bill requires standardized bidding processes, regular reporting of actual versus projected costs, audits of plan sponsors, penalties for inaccurate bids or excessive cost variances, and incorporates performance measures into star rating systems for health plans.
summary_detail.significance: The bill introduces sweeping regulations and transparency mandates across federal and commercial prescription drug programs, substantially altering how pharmacy benefit managers contract with health plans and how federal agencies audit prescription drug spending.
